title: Factors related to successful completion of a 161-km ultramarathon
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Entrants of the 2009 Western States Endurance Run and Vermont 100 (161-km trail ultramarathons); post-race questionnaire
findings: Finish time had a significant (P <= .01) negative association with training volume (higher volume, faster finish) and was generally directly associated with body mass index.
Among nonfinishers the primary reason for dropping out was nausea and/or vomiting (23.0%).

Finishers compared with nonfinishers were more likely (P <= .02) to report blisters (40.1% vs 17.3%), muscle pain (36.5% vs 20.1%) and exhaustion (23.1% vs 13.7%) as adversely affecting race performance; nausea/vomiting was similar (36.8% vs 39.6%).

Nausea/vomiting was no more common with NSAID use, higher ambient temperature, lower training volume or less 161-km finishing experience; NSAID use was high and greater (P = .006) in finishers (60.5%) than nonfinishers (46.4%). The authors concluded that the primary performance-limiting issues were nausea/vomiting, blisters and muscle pain, and that NSAID use was disturbingly high.
limitations: Self-reported retrospective questionnaire from two North American races; response and recall bias; association not causation; the abstract gives no training-volume threshold.
implications: For 100-mile plans, include a race-readiness block that rehearses the self-reported failure points: gastrointestinal tolerance of the planned fuel at race effort, foot care and blister management, and muscular conditioning for the muscle pain finishers reported (the muscle-conditioning link is an engine inference, not a tested intervention).
Treat higher weekly training volume as favourable for 100-mile finish time but do not derive a numeric minimum from this paper (none stated); direction-of-effect support only.

Include a caution note on routine NSAID use in race-day guidance: use was very high (46-61%), the authors called it disturbingly high, and nausea/vomiting was not lower in users. The study did not test NSAID benefit or harm directly.
